title: Where the Straight Line Ends: Bandpass, Reflectance and HPLC
summary: See why a photometer needs a narrow wavelength band near the absorption peak, what actually bends Beer’s law at high absorbance, how percent reflectance on a dry pad is linearised by the reader, and where high performance liquid chromatography fits, including its pressure range and haemoglobin A1c run times.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 4 Hits 4, 8 and 18 and Trap 3. Checked against Oshina 2021 (Beer–Lambert limitations), Sasagawa 2018 (interference vs absorption filters), Costa 2021 (thin-film bandpass filter design), Oyaert 2019a and 2019b (reflectometry and automated strip analysis), Dai 2018 (Kubelka–Munk linear region), Yabré 2018 (conventional vs ultra-high-pressure LC), Park 2019 (ion-exchange HPLC HbA1c turnaround) and Douzi 2026 (NGSP reference method). Not taught as fact: the reviewer’s interference-filter bandwidth of about 1.5% of the peak wavelength and the 30–50 nm figure for colored-glass absorption filters, the fixed A < 2.0 linearity ceiling, the ~6000 PSI figure as an HPLC maximum, and the “HbA1c within 5 min” figure; see accuracy flags and register flags rv-ch4-filter-bandwidth-figures, rv-ch4-beer-fixed-ceiling and rv-ch4-hplc-pressure-ceiling. Chapter 4 Number Vault (table1) is not taught: this lesson covers only a few of its rows.

objectives: Explain why a photometer’s wavelength band must be narrow and placed near the absorption maximum, and how an interference filter differs in mechanism from a dye absorption filter.
Name the optical and chemical reasons a measured absorbance stops tracking concentration at the top of the range, and state the correct laboratory response.
Describe percent reflectance as used by strip and dry-slide readers, and why the reading must be transformed before it becomes a concentration.
State the working pressure range of conventional versus ultra-high-pressure liquid chromatography and how haemoglobin A1c is measured by ion-exchange chromatography.

scenes.title: Off the end of the line
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a glucose assay on a filter photometer returns an absorbance of 2.6, well past the top calibrator, and a trainee argues that because Beer’s law is a straight line the concentration can simply be read further along it. On the next bench a urine strip reader has reported protein 2+ from a percent reflectance reading, and the same trainee assumes reflectance is just absorbance upside down. Question token: “Where does the straight line end?”

cues.text: A glucose assay comes back with an absorbance of two point six, far above the top calibrator.
A trainee says Beer’s law is a straight line, so just read the concentration further along it. On the next bench, a strip reader has turned a reflectance reading into protein two plus.
So where does the straight line end, and what do you use once it has?

props.label: Where does the straight line end?

scenes.title: A narrow band near the peak
scenes.altText: Schematic optics diagram. The Beer–Lambert law assumes radiation that is monochromatic, collimated and normal to the sample, in a homogeneous non-scattering medium whose absorbers act independently; in practice the incident band must at least be narrower than the medium’s absorption band, and the band is chosen near the absorption maximum where absorptivity changes little with wavelength. Two wavelength selectors are drawn as schematic cards. Interference filter: alternating dielectric layers of high and low refractive index, built as a Fabry–Perot structure with two mirrors around a resonance cavity; it reflects rather than absorbs the rejected band, can form a very steep band edge, and its transmission spectrum shifts with the angle of incidence. One published eight-filter set for a reflectance device was designed for a full width at half maximum near 10 nanometres at centre wavelengths of 585 to 746 nanometres, with eleven layers per filter. Absorption (dye or pigment) filter: angle independent, absorbs the light instead of reflecting it, transmittance falling exponentially with filter thickness, and it can emit its own autofluorescence.

cues.text: Beer’s law assumes the light is monochromatic and collimated and that the sample is homogeneous and does not scatter. Real instruments cannot deliver one single wavelength, so the rule is that the band of light must be narrower than the absorption band being measured.
The band is also placed near the absorption maximum, where the absorptivity hardly changes across the band.

An interference filter stacks dielectric layers of alternating refractive index into a Fabry–Perot cavity. It reflects the wavelengths it rejects instead of absorbing them, so it can give a very steep band edge. One published eight-filter set for a reflectance analyser was designed for a width at half maximum near ten nanometres, at centre wavelengths from five hundred eighty-five to seven hundred forty-six nanometres.

A dye or pigment absorption filter is simpler and does not care about the angle of the light, but it absorbs that energy, its transmittance falls exponentially with thickness, and it can glow with its own faint fluorescence.

props.label: Sit the band near the absorption peak

scenes.title: What bends the line at the top
scenes.altText: Schematic deviation diagram. Stray radiation is light at wavelengths outside the selected band that reaches the detector after scattering or reflecting off lenses, mirrors, filters or gratings; it is not absorbed by the sample, so measured transmittance looks higher and measured absorbance reads LOWER than the true absorbance, and the absorption peak looks flattened. As concentration rises the effect grows, until transmittance can be mostly determined by the stray light rather than by the sample. Chemical causes are separate: nonlinearity appears when the absorbing species associates, dissociates or reacts with the solvent to give products with different absorption, and deviations appear in concentrated solutions and once dilute-solution ion concentration passes about 0.01 molar, where neighbouring ions are close enough to perturb one another. Instrumental causes include finite spectral resolution and an inappropriate spectral slit width, which flattens sharp absorption peaks. Conclusion card: the usable top of the curve belongs to the method, not to a universal number, and the practical move is to dilute into the validated range and multiply back by the dilution factor.

cues.text: Stray radiation is light outside the chosen band that reaches the detector after bouncing off lenses, mirrors, filters or gratings. The sample never absorbs it, so transmittance looks higher than it is and the absorbance reads lower than the truth, flattening the peak.
And the higher the concentration, the worse it gets: eventually the transmitted signal is mostly stray light, not sample.

Chemistry bends the line too. If the coloured species associates, dissociates or reacts with the solvent, the products absorb differently; concentrated solutions deviate, and in dilute solution the ions crowd one another once the concentration passes about one hundredth molar.
So the top of the usable range belongs to the method, not to one universal absorbance number: establish it by a linearity study, then dilute into that range and multiply back by the dilution factor.

props.title: Stray radiation
lines: Absorbance reads too low; peak flattens

scenes.title: Reflect it, or separate it first
scenes.altText: Schematic two-route diagram. Route one, reflectometry: automated urine strip readers and dry-slide chemistry read percent reflectance from the reagent pad, expressed as a percentage from 100 percent (white) to 0 percent (black) and inversely related to analyte concentration; by the Kubelka–Munk reflectance theory the reciprocal of the reflectance reading is proportional to the analyte concentration, with the Kubelka–Munk function equal to the absorption coefficient divided by the scattering coefficient, so the reading has to be transformed rather than read off directly. On one fully automated analyser the fitted relations were the reciprocal of reflectance against the logarithm of urine glucose and of urine protein, and two overlapping reflectance ranges were installed for pH, protein, glucose, bilirubin and ketones to hold linearity across the whole measuring range; because the scattering coefficient depends on particle size, diffuse reflectance is linear only within a region. Route two, chromatography: conventional liquid chromatography systems run to about 400 bar, roughly six thousand pounds per square inch, while ultra-high-pressure systems support above 1000 bar; cation-exchange high performance liquid chromatography is the reference method recognised by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program for haemoglobin A1c, and on evaluated ion-exchange analysers one sample took about one to one point six minutes once the two-minute sample preparation was excluded. Hook answer card.

cues.text: Route one: stop fighting the cuvette and read reflected light instead. A strip reader reports percent reflectance, one hundred percent for white down to zero for black, falling as the analyte rises. By Kubelka–Munk theory it is the reciprocal of reflectance, not reflectance itself, that tracks concentration.

So the reader linearises: on one automated analyser the reciprocal of reflectance was fitted against the logarithm of the urine glucose and protein concentration, and two overlapping reflectance ranges were installed to hold linearity across the range.

Route two: separate the analytes first. Conventional liquid chromatography pumps work to about four hundred bar, roughly six thousand pounds per square inch, and ultra-high-pressure systems go above a thousand bar. Cation-exchange chromatography is the recognised reference method for haemoglobin A1c, and evaluated ion-exchange analysers reported one sample in about one to one and a half minutes.

Back to the hook: the absorbance of two point six is outside the validated range, so dilute, re-run and multiply back; and reflectance is not absorbance flipped, it is a reciprocal relation the reader has to transform.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Beer’s law holds at any absorbance as long as you know the concentration” (✓ stray light and chemical effects bend it, and stray light dominates as concentration rises, so dilute into the validated range); “An interference filter is just a tinted glass filter” (✓ it is a dielectric multilayer that reflects the rejected band with a steep edge, and its passband shifts with the angle of incidence, while a dye filter absorbs and is angle independent); “Reflectance is proportional to concentration” (✓ percent reflectance falls from 100 to 0 and it is the reciprocal of reflectance that tracks concentration, so the reader must linearise).

cues.text: Trap one: Beer’s law holds at any absorbance if you know the concentration. No. Stray light and chemical effects bend the relation, and stray light takes over as concentration climbs, so dilute into the validated range.
Trap two: an interference filter is just tinted glass. No. It is a dielectric multilayer that reflects what it rejects, with a steep band edge, and its passband moves with the angle of the light.
Trap three: reflectance is proportional to concentration. No. Percent reflectance runs from one hundred down to zero, and it is the reciprocal of reflectance that tracks concentration.

scenes.title: The three Rs
scenes.altText: Memory aid: when a photometric signal leaves its straight-line range, use the three Rs — REDUCE it (dilute into the validated range and multiply back), REFLECT it (percent reflectance on a dry pad, which the reader linearises), or RESOLVE it (separate it on a column first). The filter rule rides along: narrow band, near the peak. Tokens: Reduce, Reflect, Resolve. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: when the signal leaves its straight-line range, use the three Rs. Reduce it by diluting into the validated range, reflect it as percent reflectance on a dry pad, or resolve it by separating it on a column first. And the filter rule rides along: narrow band, near the peak.

Where it breaks: the three Rs are a menu, not a ranking. Diluting adds imprecision and changes the matrix, reflectance carries its own interferences and is linear only where scattering stays constant, haemoglobin variants distort chromatograms, and a filter label does not guarantee the band, because an interference filter’s passband moves with the angle of the light.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Narrow band near the peak; the usable range ends where stray light and chemistry bend the line”, “Reduce (dilute, multiply back) · Reflect (1/R, reader linearises) · Resolve (separate first)”.

cues.text: A photometric reading is trustworthy only inside its validated straight-line range, because a narrow wavelength band near the absorption peak keeps the relation linear while stray light and crowded molecules bend it at high concentration, so when the signal leaves that range the laboratory dilutes it back in, switches to percent reflectance with instrument linearisation, or separates it first by high performance liquid chromatography.

props.label: Narrow band near the peak · the line ends where stray light and chemistry bend it

explanation.what: Plain language: a photometer only tells the truth over a limited stretch of its scale. It needs a narrow slice of colour, placed where the sample absorbs most strongly; past a certain concentration the reading flattens out and no longer follows the sample. Two escapes exist: read light bounced off a dry pad instead, or separate the mixture on a column before detecting it. Scientific terms: spectral bandpass, full width at half maximum, interference (dielectric multilayer, Fabry–Perot) filter, absorption filter, stray radiation, chemical deviation from the Beer–Lambert law, percent reflectance, Kubelka–Munk function, ion-exchange high performance liquid chromatography, ultra-high-pressure liquid chromatography.
explanation.why: The Beer–Lambert law is derived for monochromatic, collimated light through a homogeneous, non-scattering sample whose absorbers act independently; every real instrument breaks those assumptions a little. A wide band spans wavelengths with different absorptivities, stray light adds unabsorbed photons that matter more and more as the sample darkens, and concentrated or associating solutes change their own absorption. Reflected light obeys a different, non-proportional relation, so the instrument has to transform it. Chromatography removes the problem of overlapping absorbers altogether by separating them in time.
explanation.measure: Band: narrower than the analyte’s absorption band, placed near the absorption maximum; one published eight-filter interference set was designed for a full width at half maximum near 10 nm at centre wavelengths 585–746 nm, using 11 dielectric layers per filter. Stray light: A = log((P0+Ps)/(P+Ps)), so measured absorbance reads low and the error grows with concentration. Chemical deviation: association, dissociation or reaction with solvent; concentrated solutions, and dilute-solution ion concentrations above about 0.01 M. Reflectance: percent reflectance from 100% (white) to 0% (black), inversely related to concentration, with 1/R proportional to concentration by Kubelka–Munk, f(R) = (1−R)²/2R = k/s. Chromatography: conventional LC to about 400 bar (≈6000 psi), ultra-high-pressure systems above 1000 bar; cation-exchange HPLC is the NGSP-recognised reference method for HbA1c, and one evaluated ion-exchange analyser reported one sample in 1 minute versus 1.6 minutes for its predecessor, excluding 2 minutes of sample preparation.
explanation.differs: Interference filter (dielectric multilayer, reflects the rejected band, steep edge, angle-sensitive passband) vs absorption filter (dye or pigment, absorbs, angle-independent, exponential with thickness, can autofluoresce); transmitted absorbance (proportional to concentration within range) vs percent reflectance (reciprocal relation requiring transformation); conventional LC (about 400 bar) vs ultra-high-pressure LC (above 1000 bar).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a high absorbance with “what do you do” (dilute into range, multiply by the dilution factor, never extrapolate), a “both filters are the same” distractor, a “reflectance is proportional to concentration” distractor, or a question pairing HbA1c with ion-exchange chromatography.

mnemonic.text: When a photometric signal leaves its straight line, use the three Rs: REDUCE it (dilute into the validated range and multiply back), REFLECT it (percent reflectance on a dry pad, which the reader linearises), or RESOLVE it (separate it on a column first) — and the filter rule rides along: narrow band, near the peak.
mnemonic.explanation: Reduce = dilution into range; Reflect = reflectometry with a Kubelka–Munk style transform; Resolve = chromatographic separation before detection; “narrow band, near the peak” is the bandpass requirement that keeps the relation linear in the first place.
mnemonic.limitation: The three Rs are a menu, not a ranking: dilution adds imprecision and changes the matrix, reflectance carries its own interferences and is linear only where the scattering coefficient stays constant, haemoglobin variants distort ion-exchange chromatograms, and a filter label does not guarantee the band because an interference filter’s passband moves with the angle of incidence.

questions.stem: A colorimetric assay returns an absorbance well above the top calibrator. Which statement best explains why the reading cannot simply be extrapolated?

options.text: Stray radiation that the sample does not absorb makes the measured absorbance read low, and this error grows as concentration rises
options.rationale: Correct. Stray light raises apparent transmittance so measured absorbance falls below the true value, and as concentration increases the transmitted signal can be mostly stray light rather than sample.

options.text: The path length of the cuvette shortens at high concentration
options.rationale: Incorrect. Path length is a fixed geometric property of the cuvette and does not change with the concentration of the sample.

options.text: Absorptivity is a universal constant, so the curve can always be extended
options.rationale: Incorrect. Absorptivity is wavelength and chemistry dependent, and the point of the question is that the relation stops being linear, so extrapolation is exactly what must not be done.

options.text: The detector becomes more sensitive at high absorbance
options.rationale: Incorrect. Detector response is not improved by a darker sample; limited spectral resolution and non-linear detector response are listed among the instrumental sources of error, not benefits.

questions.stem: How does an interference filter differ in mechanism from a colored-glass absorption filter?

options.text: It is a stack of dielectric layers of alternating refractive index that reflects the rejected band, and its passband shifts with the angle of incidence
options.rationale: Correct. Interference filters are built from alternating dielectric multilayers, reflect rather than absorb the rejected wavelengths so they emit almost no autofluorescence, and their transmission spectrum shifts with the incident angle.

options.text: It uses a dye that absorbs unwanted wavelengths, and its transmission is independent of the incident angle
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes an absorption filter, whose dyes or pigments absorb the light and whose transmission spectrum is angle independent.

options.text: It disperses light by refraction, like a prism, so the band is selected by moving a slit
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is a dispersing monochromator, not a filter; the filter selects a band by thin-film interference rather than by angular dispersion.

options.text: It converts light to an electrical signal, replacing the photodetector
options.rationale: Incorrect. A filter is a wavelength selector in the light path; detection is a separate step performed by a photodiode or photomultiplier.

questions.stem: An automated urine strip reader reports results from percent reflectance readings. Which statement about that measurement is correct?

options.text: Reflectance runs from 100% for white to 0% for black and is inversely related to concentration, with the reciprocal of reflectance proportional to analyte concentration
options.rationale: Correct. Readers express reflectance as a percentage from 100% (white) to 0% (black) that falls as analyte rises, and by Kubelka–Munk reflectance theory the reciprocal of the reflectance reading is proportional to the concentration.

options.text: Reflectance is directly proportional to concentration, so it can be reported without transformation
options.rationale: Incorrect. The relation is inverse and non-proportional; instruments fit the reciprocal of reflectance against the logarithm of concentration and may install overlapping reflectance ranges to hold linearity.

options.text: Reflectance measurements obey the Beer–Lambert law directly because the light passes through the pad
options.rationale: Incorrect. The measurement is of light returned from a scattering pad, described by reflectance theory in which the scattering coefficient matters, not by simple transmission through a clear solution.

options.text: Reflectance readings are independent of the scattering properties of the pad
options.rationale: Incorrect. In the Kubelka–Munk function the measured quantity equals the absorption coefficient divided by the scattering coefficient, and the scattering coefficient varies with particle size, so scattering matters a great deal.

Conventional liquid chromatography systems work to about 400 bar (roughly 6000 psi) while ultra-high-pressure systems support above 1000 bar; cation-exchange HPLC is the NGSP-recognised reference method for haemoglobin A1c, and evaluated ion-exchange analysers reported one sample in about 1 to 1.6 minutes excluding sample preparation.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer states an interference-filter bandwidth of about 1.5% of the peak wavelength and 30–50 nm for colored-glass absorption filters. No open source read in this session states either as a general specification; the published eight-filter interference set read here was designed for a full width at half maximum near 10 nm at centre wavelengths of 585–746 nm and measured above 10 nm after fabrication. The figures are taught here only as the order of magnitude of a narrow bandpass, not as specifications.

The reviewer presents absorbance 2.0 as the point where Beer’s law linearity fails. The source read describes deviation as the sum of instrument-specific and chemistry-specific effects — stray radiation (which grows with concentration), spectral bandwidth and slit width, chemical equilibria, refractive index and high solute concentration — so the usable ceiling is method dependent and established by a linearity study rather than fixed at 2.0.

The reviewer gives ~6000 PSI as the HPLC pump maximum and “HbA1c within 5 min”. The sources read put about 400 bar (≈6000 psi) as the conventional liquid chromatography limit, with ultra-high-pressure systems supporting above 1000 bar, and report single-sample HbA1c turnaround on ion-exchange analysers of 1 minute versus 1.6 minutes for an older model, excluding two minutes of sample preparation.
